items.title: India Amends Foreign Contribution Regulation Rules with Stringent New Requirements for NGOs
items.summary: On June 22, 2026, India's Ministry of Home Affairs amended the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011, introducing significant new restrictions on organizations receiving foreign contributions. The amended rules require organizations registered under FCRA seeking renewal or holding prior permission to submit new disclosures and comply with stringent regulations including activity and geographic limitations, bars on foreign national involvement, expanded compliance obligations, increased reporting and monitoring requirements, and new spending and utilization thresholds. This follows a March 2026 draft amendment proposal that included provisions for state seizure of non-profit assets even if only partially foreign-funded. These changes reflect a highly controlling regulatory approach that will substantially increase compliance burdens for non-profits receiving foreign funds, particularly smaller and grassroots organizations. The amendments raise serious concerns under international law and do not appear compliant with Financial Action Task Force (FATF) recommendations, significantly impacting the operational capacity and resources of India's civil society sector. In March 2026, the Government of India introduced the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha, proposing major structural changes to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010. The bill creates a new regulatory framework governing foreign contributions and assets when an organization's registration is suspended, cancelled, surrendered, or lapsed. Under the proposed changes, foreign-funded assets would be provisionally vested in a government-designated authority, which may assume control over their management and, if registration is not restored within a prescribed period, permanently take ownership of those assets. The authority would also be empowered to transfer such assets to government entities or dispose of them, with proceeds directed to the public treasury. Additional regulatory changes include formalizing automatic cessation of registration where renewal is not obtained, expanding the definition of 'key functionaries' subject to compliance requirements and potential liability, and establishing time-bound conditions for the receipt and use of foreign contributions under prior permission. In early April 2026, parliamentary consideration of the bill was deferred to a subsequent legislative session following opposition from political parties and concerns raised by stakeholders, including religious groups. This development represents a significant shift toward a more centralized, asset-focused regulatory approach that extends beyond oversight of funding flows to risk organizational continuity and control of resources, with potentially substantial implications for Indian civil society organizations and their donors. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman introduced the Finance (No. 2) Bill 2024 in the Lok Sabha on July 23, 2024. The proposed amendments will not adversely affect NPOs/NGOs overall. The phasing out of the tax regime under section 10(23C)(iv), (v), (vi), or (via) is not expected to significantly impact the sector since most NPOs/NGOs are registered under Section 12(AB). The requirements and benefits of tax exemption under both sections are nearly identical. Importantly, institutions already registered under 10(23C)(iv), (v), (vi), or (via) will not lose their existing benefits concerning modes of investment upon making the transition. This update is significant for the Indian nonprofit sector as it clarifies that recent tax law changes will maintain stability and continuity for existing registered organizations while simplifying the regulatory framework. On October 19, 2022, the Supreme Court of India ruled in Civil Appeal No. 21762 OF 2017 that organizations engaged in revenue-generating activities under the category of 'advancement of other object of general public utility' must demonstrate that such activities are incidental to their charitable purpose and not profit-oriented to maintain tax-exempt status. This ruling clarifies earlier amendments allowing income-generating activities if they are undertaken in the course of carrying out general public utility purposes and aggregate receipts do not exceed 20 percent of total receipts. Concurrently, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) issued a Notification on August 10, 2022, introducing Rule 17AA to the Income Tax Rules, detailing mandatory books and financial records required of all tax-exempt entities. Additionally, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) issued Notification G.S.R. 715(E) on September 20, 2022, amending CSR Policy Rules to broaden eligibility for CSR implementing agencies to include trusts, societies, and Section 8 companies registered under Section 10(23C)(iv)-(vi) of the Income Tax Act, alongside those registered under Section 12AB. These regulatory updates significantly impact Indian NGOs by clarifying compliance requirements for tax exemption, establishing stricter financial record-keeping standards, and expanding opportunities for organizations to serve as CSR implementing agencies. India enacted significant regulatory changes in 2019 affecting NGO operations and tax status. The Finance Act, 2019 empowered the Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Income Tax to cancel tax-exemption registration under Section 12AA if organizations violate any law, subjecting them to income tax at the maximum marginal rate of 30 percent and tax on accrued income. The Taxation Laws Amendment Act, 2019 introduced a reduced corporate income-tax rate for companies forgoing exemptions, which reduced tax incentives for donations to NGOs as many companies opted for the lower rate. The National Investigation Agency (NIA) Bill, 2019, passed by the Lok Sabha on July 15, 2019, expanded NIA's investigative authority to include human trafficking, counterfeit currency, prohibited arms, cyber-terrorism, and offenses under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, with authority to investigate scheduled offenses committed outside India. On September 16, 2019, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued Notification G.S.R. 659(E) requiring office bearers, key functionaries, and governing-body members of FCRA-registered organizations to submit affidavits in a prescribed format. These developments have significant implications for NGO governance, financial sustainability, and operational autonomy in India's social-impact sector. On June 22, 2026, the Government of India amended the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011, introducing significant new compliance obligations and operational restrictions for organizations receiving foreign funding. The amendments require organizations to identify specific purposes and geographic locations (States or Union Territories) for FCRA registration from a government-prescribed schedule of over 100 approved religious, cultural, economic, educational, and social activities. Existing registrants must notify the government of purposes and areas for which they wish to retain registration, while expansion into new purposes or locations requires approval. The schedule expressly excludes proselytization and religious conversion from permitted religious activities. The Rules broaden the definition of 'key functionary' to include trustees, directors, partners, and office bearers, and generally prohibit organizations with foreign nationals in key functionary positions from obtaining registration unless specifically authorized by the government. While the amendments did not adopt certain controversial measures from the March 2026 FCRA Amendment Bill (such as vesting NGO assets in the government upon loss of FCRA registration), they significantly expand administrative controls over foreign-funded civil society organizations and raise concerns regarding consistency with international standards and Financial Action Task Force recommendations. This development has major implications for Indian NGOs and the social-impact sector, as it increases regulatory scrutiny, limits operational flexibility, and may affect the ability of international organizations to collaborate with Indian counterparts. In December 2015, India's Ministry of Home Affairs amended the Foreign Contribution Regulation Rules, implementing major changes that substantially increased compliance and reporting burdens for NGOs receiving foreign contributions. Key amendments include: mandatory online submission of registration, prior-permission, and renewal applications through revised Form FC-3 with digital signatures (ending postal applications); annual online publication of audited accounts by all foreign-contribution recipients within nine months of the financial year-end; annual Form FC-4 filing with affirmations that foreign funds were not used for activities prejudicial to sovereignty, security, or public interest; quarterly disclosure of donor names, amounts, and receipt dates within 15 days after each quarter (requirement remained until July 2022); bank notification requirements within 48 hours of any foreign contribution; and NGO notification requirements within 45 days of changes to name, address, objectives, or key members. These amendments significantly impact India's social-impact sector by increasing administrative burden, particularly for smaller organizations and those operating across multiple regions, while raising concerns about transparency requirements and government oversight of civil society organizations. On June 22, 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Rules, 2026, further tightening access to resources for foreign-funded organizations in India. The new rules require FCRA-registered organizations to identify approved purposes and geographic areas for foreign-funded activities, with government approval required for any subsequent changes. The amendments expand reporting and disclosure obligations, introduce additional donor-transparency requirements, bar organizations with foreign nationals as key functionaries from receiving FCRA approval, and impose new spending and utilization thresholds for maintaining registration and receiving future installments of foreign funding. Civil society groups have raised concerns that these amendments significantly increase compliance burdens and further restrict access to foreign funding, particularly affecting smaller organizations and those operating across multiple regions, thereby impacting the broader social-impact sector's ability to access international resources. New criminal laws came into effect in India on July 1, 2024, replacing the Indian Penal Code of 1860, the 1973 Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Indian Evidence Act of 1872. The new laws contain concerning provisions that replace sedition clauses with a new clause punishing 'acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India' and increasing the minimum punishment for violations to seven years. Other provisions raise due process, privacy, and free expression concerns. Amnesty International and other NGOs have called for the laws' repeal. Police in Uttar Pradesh used the new penal code to charge journalists who reported on the alleged mob lynching of a Muslim resident shortly after the criminal laws took effect. These changes have significant implications for Indian NGOs and civil society organizations, as the broader definitions and increased penalties could be used to restrict advocacy work, journalism, and peaceful dissent. On June 22, 2026, India's Ministry of Home Affairs adopted the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Rules granting the Indian government sweeping new powers to police the activities, operation, management and leadership of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) receiving foreign funding. The new rules apply to nearly 14,500 organizations that currently hold a FCRA license, and to all non-profits who may want to apply in the future. Existing non-profit organizations now face a one-year deadline to bring their registration in line with a far more limiting framework, or risk losing the ability to carry out their work altogether. This regulatory update significantly impacts the social-impact sector by restricting NGO autonomy and foreign funding access, creating compliance challenges for civil society organizations across India. The Enforcement Directorate (ED) conducted raids on eight locations linked to three Bengaluru-based companies that received funds from the US nonprofit Open Society Foundations (OSF), backed by US billionaire George Soros, in alleged contravention of Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) rules. The OSF transferred Rs 25 crore to the companies in suspicious transactions in recent months. The ED will review transaction details and file an Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) if any hint of money laundering is found. This action reflects India's ongoing scrutiny of foreign funding to NGOs and civil society organizations, which has significant implications for the social-impact sector's ability to receive international support. Thousands of civil society groups in India have had their licenses to receive overseas donations cancelled since Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government tightened surveillance on non-profit groups regulated under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA). According to the government's FCRA dashboard, only 15,947 NGOs with an FCRA licence are still active, while permissions for 35,488 NGOs have either been cancelled or have expired and not been renewed. This crisis has left many organizations struggling to survive and vulnerable populations lacking vital services. The example of BSFC, a medical NGO that provided critical surgical services, illustrates the impact—its license to receive foreign funds expired in October 2021 and has not been renewed since. The widespread cancellations and non-renewals of FCRA licenses represent a significant constraint on India's civil society sector and its ability to deliver essential services to 1.4 billion people. The Indian government has proposed legislation to overhaul colonial-era criminal and penal laws introduced during British rule. On the last day of the monsoon session of parliament, Union Home Minister Amit Shah introduced three bills to repeal and replace the Indian Penal Code, the Code of Criminal Procedure, and the Indian Evidence Act. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita will replace the Indian Penal Code of 1860; the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita will replace the Code of Criminal Procedure; and the Bharatiya Sakshya Bill will replace the Indian Evidence Act. This legislative overhaul affects the legal framework governing civil society organizations and their operations in India. India's Enforcement Directorate (ED) and Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) conducted multiple raids against major international NGOs Amnesty International and Greenpeace between October 2018 and November 2019, citing alleged violations of the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA). On October 25, 2018, the ED raided Amnesty International's Bengaluru offices, confiscating documents and laptops, alleging that Amnesty circumvented FCRA restrictions by establishing a commercial entity (AIIPL) that received Rs 36 crore in foreign funds through commercial channels, including Rs 10 crore as long-term loans placed in fixed deposits. The ED contended that Amnesty masked foreign donations as commercial payments for services to evade FCRA restrictions. Similarly, on October 5, 2018, Greenpeace's offices were raided and bank accounts frozen for alleged FCRA violations and fraudulent fundraising; Greenpeace's FCRA registration had been cancelled in 2015 on grounds of 'anti-national activities.' On November 15, 2019, the CBI conducted further raids on Amnesty's offices, alleging that Amnesty International UK had transferred INR 46 crore classified as Foreign Direct Investment rather than foreign contribution. Both organizations denied wrongdoing, with Amnesty stating it stood in full compliance with Indian and international law. By September 2020, Amnesty International closed its operations in India due to government pressure. These enforcement actions represent a significant crackdown on civil society organizations and have major implications for NGO operations, foreign funding mechanisms, and civic freedoms in India.
